title: Nyaya (logic)
hook: a gray column rises behind the next hill, nobody can see a flame, and everybody says fire

segments.voice: Yesterday we opened Nyaya, the school of logic, with its four means of knowing: perception, inference, comparison, and the word of someone reliable. What did you catch yourself repeating as fact? Today, one of the four, up close. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.
screen: `NYAYA: FOUR MEANS OF KNOWING.` · `ONE OF THEM, UP CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Three friends are walking a ridge in the late afternoon. Across the valley, from behind the next hill, a gray column is rising, leaning a little with the wind. Nobody can see a flame. The hill is in the way. And yet all three say the same word at once: fire. Somebody's burning something over there. Nobody doubts it, and nobody stops to wonder how they knew a thing none of them can see. Nyaya stops right there. That small, quick leap from what you see to what you don't is one of its four means of knowing, and the hill with smoke on it is the example its teachers reach for.
screen: `A GRAY COLUMN, NO FLAME.` → `ALL THREE SAY FIRE.` → `HOW DID THEY KNOW?`

segments.voice: The word is anumana: inference, knowing something you can't see by way of a sign you can. Nyaya teachers lay it out in plain pieces. The hill has fire. Because it has smoke. And here's what makes that work: smoke and fire have been seen together before, at the kitchen hearth, again and again. The opposite has been seen too: a still lake, no fire, no smoke. From cases like those comes a rule: wherever there's smoke, there's fire. Later Nyaya teachers gave that rule its own name, vyapti, pervasion: the smoke is always found inside the territory of fire. With the rule in hand, the leap across the valley isn't a guess. It's knowing. But Nyaya is just as interested in how the leap goes wrong. The Nyaya Sutra names reasons that only look like reasons, and teachers give homely examples. One trap: the sign isn't what you think. That gray column might be mist rising off the trees, or dust from a road. Same color, no fire. Before you reason from smoke, make sure it's smoke. A second trap: the rule runs backward. Wherever there's smoke, there's fire. True. But wherever there's fire, there's smoke? A red-hot iron ball glows with fire and gives off no smoke at all. The rule only runs one way. Away from the ridge, these traps turn up all the time. A closed office door, so the boss is angry. A short reply, so they don't care. Maybe. Or maybe it's mist. Nyaya doesn't ask you to stop inferring. You couldn't live a day without it. It asks two questions before the leap: is the sign real? And does the rule really run this way?
screen: `ANUMANA: FROM A SIGN TO THE UNSEEN.` · `SMOKE AND FIRE AT THE HEARTH.` · `IS IT SMOKE, OR MIST?` · `THE RULE RUNS ONE WAY.` · then, large: `IS THE SIGN REAL?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one leap. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a conclusion you reached this week about someone, from a sign: a look, a silence, a tone of voice. Hold the sign in front of you. Ask the first question: was it really what I took it for, or could it have been mist? Then ask the second: does my rule really run this way? Do I know that this sign always comes with that meaning? Don't decide anything. Just let the leap slow down until you can see it. If you pray, you can ask the God you know for clear eyes. The bell holds the time.
Nyaya. Today, anumana, inference: the hill has fire because it has smoke, as long as it's really smoke, and the rule really runs that way.
Your line: Nyaya, logic. Today, when you catch yourself jumping to a conclusion about someone, ask: is it smoke, or is it mist? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: In traditional Sanskrit study, students of Nyaya learn inference through the example of smoke and fire on a hill, practicing how to state a sign, a rule and a supporting case, and how to spot reasons that only look like reasons.

original.note: Sanskrit: anumana, inference, one of Nyaya's means of knowing.

trapdoor: what you thought: inference is just guessing.
what it means: reasoning from a sign you can see to something you can't, which holds only if the sign is real and the rule runs the right way.
what a scholar hears: the hill has fire because it has smoke, as at a hearth; later Nyaya names the rule vyapti, and the red-hot iron ball shows it doesn't run backward.

notes: Second Nyaya day. Takes inference (smoke and fire), which day 1162 deliberately left aside; 1162's review asks where the listener jumped to a conclusion, which this carry sets up.

The smoke-fire example, the hearth (mahanasa) and lake (hrada) cases, mist or dust mistaken for smoke, and the red-hot iron ball (ayogolaka) are from the later Nyaya teaching tradition (e.g. Tarkasangraha), not the Sutra's own words; attributed to 'Nyaya teachers'. Confirm.
'Vyapti' is attributed to 'later Nyaya teachers'; confirm it is fair not to place it in the Sutra.
Nyaya Sutra 1.2.4 lists the hetvabhasas; the script does not count them.
